analysis.one_liner: Imposes a $2 billion annual fee on opioid manufacturers to fund addiction treatment.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in December 2018, referred to the Senate health committee, and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require companies that made opioid painkillers since 1999 to pay an annual fee totaling $2 billion, split among them based on how much of the opioid market each held. Addiction-treatment drugs and opioids for cancer and hospice patients would be exempt. The money would go to federal block grants that pay for local substance abuse prevention and treatment programs.
analysis.who_benefits: Communities hit by the opioid epidemic: the fee money would flow into the Substance Abuse Prevention and Treatment Block Grant, which funds state and local treatment, prevention, and recovery services. Taxpayers also benefit because treatment would be paid for by the companies that sold the drugs rather than by general revenue.

how_it_helps.text: Each of the 10 years after enactment, the Secretary of Health and Human Services would assess fees on prescription drug manufacturers that made opioids, totaling $2 billion a year and apportioned by each company's share of the opioid market.
The fee is retroactive in reach: it applies to any manufacturer that made opioids at any time from January 1, 1999 onward, not just current producers.
Drugs used exclusively to treat opioid addiction as part of medically assisted treatment, and opioids for cancer or hospice patients, would be exempt so the fee does not raise the cost of treatment.
All fee revenue would be transferred to the Substance Abuse Prevention and Treatment Block Grant under the Public Health Service Act, funding state and local prevention and treatment programs.

analysis.who_pays: Opioid manufacturers, including companies that sold opioid painkillers at any point since 1999, would pay the annual fee based on their market share. To the extent companies pass costs forward, patients using opioids outside the exempt categories could face somewhat higher prices.

drawbacks.text: The fee is retroactive in character: it charges companies for past lawful sales of products that were legal to manufacture and prescribe, which critics would call punishing companies for conduct that was not illegal at the time.
At $2 billion a year, the fee is small relative to the scale of the opioid crisis and the cost of treating it, so it would supplement rather than transform the treatment system.

Drug companies could raise prices on remaining opioid products to offset the fee, shifting some of the cost to patients with legitimate pain needs, though addiction-treatment and cancer/hospice opioids are exempt.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is straightforward: new, dedicated money for addiction treatment paid by the companies that built the opioid market, with exemptions protecting treatment drugs and end-of-life care. The main costs are the fairness question of charging companies for past legal sales and the risk of modest price pass-through. As drafted the fee is a meaningful supplement to treatment funding, not a cure for the epidemic's scale, and it was never refined or debated because it received no action.

outcome.mechanism: Senator Merkley introduced the bill in December 2018, it was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, and it died there without a single cosponsor and no vote before the Congress ended in early January 2019.

narrative.text: Senator Jeff Merkley introduced the Opioid Treatment Surge Act in the Senate on December 5, 2018.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day, which was the only action it ever received.
No senator cosponsored the bill; the cosponsor list was empty.
The 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, and the bill never received a markup, a committee vote, or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Opioid manufacturers are better off: no $2 billion annual fee was ever assessed, and the treatment block grant got no new revenue from them. The bill cost its sponsor nothing beyond the introduction itself.

for.name: Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Opioid Treatment Surge Act on December 5, 2018; the bill never drew a cosponsor.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction under Chairman Lamar Alexander (R-TN)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill on the day it was introduced and took no further action: no markup, no committee vote, and no floor consideration during the remaining month of the Congress.

against.name: The Senate as a whole
against.role: 99 other senators, none of whom joined as cosponsors
against.what_they_did: No senator from either party cosponsored the bill during its month of existence.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no other senator of either party cosponsored, so the bill's fate reflects a lack of support across the board rather than a party split.

industries.note: The bill would have charged each manufacturer an annual fee of up to $2 billion apportioned by its share of the opioid market, reaching back to companies that sold opioids since 1999. It died without a vote, so these companies never paid it.
All fee revenue would have gone to the Substance Abuse Prevention and Treatment Block Grant, which funds state and local treatment and prevention services. The funding never materialized.

industries.industry: Drugmakers of addiction-treatment and cancer/hospice opioids
industries.note: Drugs used exclusively for medication-assisted addiction treatment and for cancer or hospice patients were exempt from the fee, protecting those products' costs and markets.
